old_title: Iran war live: Vance says 'things happen' after US accused of wedding strike
new_title: Iran war live: Vance says 'things happen' after US accused of wedding strike
old_text:
JD Vance has faced backlash after appearing to dismiss reports that a US strike killed five people, including two children, at a wedding gathering in southern Iran.
When asked about whether a US strike was responsible, he said "sometimes things happen".
He said: "I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what's happened in the conflict thus far, so I'm extremely sceptical of this."
The toll was confirmed not by the Iranian government but by the Iranian Red Crescent, a member of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement.
"What I can say with 100% confidence is that, unlike the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC, the United States never targets civilians in combat," Vance said. "We never will do that. We never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen."
Meanwhile, president Donald Trump insisted he had done the "right thing" with the war.
It comes amid fears Trump is planning to extend Washington's war on Iran, after The Wall Street Journal reported that the Pentagon was extending the presence of troops in the Middle East into next year.
Araghchi defends Iran over strikes on Jordan
Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi takes to social media to respond to his Jordanian counterpart's recent comments criticising Iran for strikes on Jordan and neighbouring countries.
The Jordanian minister Ayman Safadi said that attacks on his country came within two hours of the start of the war, in February, suggesting the attack was not reactionary.
Araghchi writes: "How much time does the Jordanian Foreign Minister believe Iran should wait before responding to an aggressor that respects neither Arab sovereignty nor Iranian sovereignty?"
He adds: "And is he truly unaware that Arab airspace, lands, and waters were used in the initial American attacks that resulted in the killing of innocent Iranians?"
Evidence points to US weapon in deadly strike on Iran wedding celebration
The United States is investigating a deadly strike on a wedding gathering in southern Iran after weapons experts reviewing verified images and video concluded the blast was likely caused by a direct hit from a U.S. munition, Vice President JD Vance said Thursday.
Five people have died following Tuesday's strike on a home hosting the celebration, according to Iranian state television, which reported Thursday that a 22-year-old woman had died from her injuries. Iranian officials said nearly 70 others were wounded.
Speaking to reporters Thursday, Vance confirmed U.S. authorities were examining what happened.
"We're investigating it because obviously we care. We want to know," Vance said.
Trump claims US has 'unlimited' munitions amid Iran war concerns
Donald Trump has denied persistent reports that the Iran war has dangerously depleted the U.S. weapons stockpile, blasting the media for what he claimed was false reporting on the state of the American arsenal.
"For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War (which is highly unlikely!), that could improbably take place," he wrote Thursday on Truth Social.
"In addition, we are producing Munitions at levels never seen before," he added. "We are stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen."
In focus: Sailors on USS Abraham Lincoln describe 'the worst deployment'
US service members assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln are speaking out about their record-long, nearly nine-month deployment at sea, during which they supported the ongoing Iran war.
The Nimitz-class aircraft carrier - some of whose crew had reportedly suffered from deteriorating mental health - laid anchor off Thailand this week, affording its 5,000 sailors and Marines their first port call in 286 days.
While on shore in the resort town of Pattaya, some service members spoke with MS NOW Pentagon Correspondent Priya Sridhar, who recounted her discussions with them during a subsequent on-camera interview.

This morning: Asian benchmarks mostly rise after tech stocks lead rally on Wall Street
Asian shares were mostly higher in early Friday trading, as regional market sentiment got a boost from the rally on Wall Street, mostly from big technology stocks.
Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 rose 0.6% in morning trading to 64,622.33. South Korea's Kospi gained 0.9% to 6,635.67. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was little changed, slipping less than 0.1% to 9,011.80. Hong Kong's Hang Seng jumped 2.1% to 25,751.26, while the Shanghai Composite added 0.8% to 3,973.27.
Stocks on Wall Street closed higher Thursday as a recent run-up in bond yields eased further and big technology companies rallied. The S&P 500 rose 1.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1.2%, and the Nasdaq composite closed 1.4% higher.
The latest:
Shipping traffic through Hormuz well below normal, Kpler data says
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained well below normal on Thursday, with only four commodity vessels crossing the key waterway, according to preliminary Kpler data cited by Reuters.
That was down from nine crossings the day before and well below the 10-day average of about 15.
The vessels included two medium-range tankers, a Kamsarmax tanker and a Handysize vessel.
Vance refuses to give a deadline to end US war on Iran
JD Vance has declined to give a timeline for ending the US war on Iran, while downplaying the conflict by saying there was no active shooting and major combat had lasted only about six weeks.
"I wouldn't call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting," Vance said. He added: "I recognise there have been places where this has flared up."
"When you ask, 'When will this end?', you're asking me a question like: When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?" Vance told reporters.
"I think the reality is, I don't know the answer to that question. You'd have to ask the Iranians."
His remarks come after days of intense fighting between the US and Iran.
Israel says economic pressure on Iran could push the regime to take 'desperate steps'
Israel's defence minister has warned that growing economic pressure could push Tehran to take more desperate measures.
"We see signs indicating that the heavy economic pressure they are under, and the fear of an uprising and the collapse of the regime, may push them to desperate steps," Israel Katz said.
Earlier, Iran had claimed that it had the capability to manufacture more missile stockpiles and maintained enough in its war against the US"Initially, some believed that Iran had only a limited number of missiles and that its stockpiles would eventually be depleted as the war continued," the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Brig Gen Hossein Mohebbi said.
"However, that assumption proved incorrect, as Iran's missile capability has remained sustained and its missile production has continued."
Trump rejects reports of US weapons stockpiles running low
Donald Trump has rejected reports that US military stockpiles of weapons are running dangerously low as the war with Iran enters its seventh month.
In a post on his Truth Social platform he wrote that the US was producing munitions at "levels never seen before" and has "far more than we could ever use".
"For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War (which is highly unlikely!), that could improbably take place," Trump wrote.
"In addition, we are producing Munitions at levels never seen before. We are stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen. We are taking them for ourselves, the U.S.A., rather than selling them to others, but the sales to Allies will soon again, begin. Also, please let it be known, that the Biden Administration gave far more Munitions away to Ukraine, at no cost to them, whatsoever, than we have used in Iran."

Trump to use $400M Qatari gift plane for international trips despite security concerns
President Donald Trump plans to fly to Ireland next week on the Boeing 747 donated by Qatar, despite concerns over its security and unfinished upgrades, a senior White House official told the Washington Post.
The trip will mark Trump's first international journey on the Qatari jet since U.S. officials secretly moved him to another plane during his return from July's NATO summit in Turkey after intelligence indicated a potential Iranian threat.
"We don't comment on specific upgrades or modifications to Air Force One," a senior administration official told the Post. "We maintain a consistent posture that ensures a safe, secure, and reliable capability for the President of the United States and routinely evolve the capability as required to maintain that posture."

The Trump administration has not accepted responsibility for the strike, which came amid a new escalation in the conflict as President Donald Trump faces growing domestic pressure to end the fighting ahead of November's midterm elections.
ICYMI: What happened in suspected US strike which hit Iran wedding?
At least four people were killed in a suspected US attack that hit a wedding in Iran after Tehran and Washington exchanged the heaviest strikes between them since July.
The Iranian Red Crescent (IRC) has asked the International Criminal Court to investigate the incident, calling for "an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation" due to the "civilian character of the location". Iran has accused the US of "war crimes", but the US maintains that it does not target civilians.
The Independent looks at how the attack took place and what both parties have said about it.
US in turmoil: Trump faces Iran war nightmare as diesel hits record $5.85 and prices threaten to soar
Fuel costs hit an unprecedented high in the U.S. on Friday, with diesel soaring to a record national average of $5.85 a gallon as an ongoing six-month war with Iran continues to disrupt global fuel flows.
Because freight and delivery networks rely heavily on diesel, these rising expenses mean higher transportation costs for a vast array of everyday consumer goods.
Commercial enterprises across multiple sectors are absorbing steeper bills, with several already passing the burden on to buyers through added fees on online orders and packages in the mail. Consequently, shoppers are likely to see increasing sticker shock trickle onto store shelves.

Iranian officials acknowledge in private that US pressure is working
Three senior Iranian sources have told the Reuters news agency that the US campaign to throttle Iran's economy by blockading its oil exports is growing increasingly difficult to withstand.
While Iran's clerical rulers have managed to get around harsh sanctions for decades, the latest US movements have left them in a far more sensitive position, with few remaining channels to secure foreign currency or buy goods, the sources said.
Iran publicly maintains that it has plenty foreign currency reserves and is not meaningfully affected by the US crackdown on sanctions evasion.
The latest measures expanded secondary sanctions that target countries doing business with Iran in a bid to stop it clearing dollar transactions needed for both oil sales and to finance crucial imports of goods and raw materials.
That effort is making Iran's existing sanctions evasion networks - front companies, unregistered tankers and smuggling - too expensive to use, the three senior sources said.
One of the sources said Iran only has another two months' supply of gasoline, which has to be imported due to limited refining capacity.
